reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: Rare malignant neuroectodermal tumour arising from the olfactory neuroepithelium high in the nasal vault (cribriform plate, superior turbinate, upper septum).
Classic bimodal age distribution with peaks in the second and sixth decades, and no strong sex predilection.
Typical presentation is unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis; hyposmia or anosmia is frequent but often unnoticed by the patient.
A dumbbell-shaped mass straddling the cribriform plate with intracranial and intranasal components is a characteristic imaging appearance.
Kadish staging (A confined to nasal cavity, B nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, C extension beyond, D nodal or distant disease) and Hyams histological grade together drive prognosis and management.
Histology shows small round blue cells in lobules with neurofibrillary stroma, Homer Wright and occasionally Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes.
Immunohistochemistry shows synaptophysin and chromogranin positivity with S100-positive sustentacular cells at lobule peripheries and usually negative or only focal cytokeratin.
Craniofacial or expanded endoscopic resection with negative skull-base margins plus adjuvant radiotherapy is the mainstay; late neck-node and delayed local recurrence mandate prolonged surveillance.
reference.pathophysiology: The tumour arises from the basal neuronal precursor cells of the olfactory neuroepithelium lining the roof of the nasal cavity, showing malignant neuroectodermal and neuroendocrine differentiation. It grows in an organoid lobular pattern within a neurofibrillary matrix and characteristically erodes the cribriform plate to invade the anterior cranial fossa, dura and orbit; cysts at the tumour-brain interface are a helpful marker of intracranial spread. Hyams grading (I to IV) reflects preservation of lobular architecture, degree of rosette formation, mitotic activity, nuclear pleomorphism and the presence of necrosis, with higher grades behaving more aggressively.
additionalDifferentials: Sinonasal neuroendocrine or small cell carcinoma
Olfactory groove meningioma or pituitary adenoma
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy with representative biopsy of the vault mass
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the paranasal sinuses and brain to define dural, intracranial and orbital extension and interface cysts
High-resolution CT of the sinuses to assess cribriform plate and lamina papyracea erosion
Immunohistochemistry panel (synaptophysin, chromogranin, S100 sustentacular pattern, cytokeratin) to confirm diagnosis
Whole-body PET-CT for staging and detection of distant disease
Neck imaging and ultrasound for regional nodal assessment
Ophthalmology review with visual fields where orbital involvement is suspected
redFlags: Intracranial or dural extension with headache, altered mental state or CSF rhinorrhoea
Orbital invasion causing proptosis, diplopia or visual loss
New or enlarging neck lump suggesting nodal metastasis
Progressive unilateral nasal obstruction with epistaxis and anosmia in an adult
reference.prognosis: Low Kadish stage and low Hyams grade with complete craniofacial resection and adjuvant radiotherapy carry a favourable long-term outlook. Higher stage, high grade, dural or intracranial extension and nodal spread worsen survival, and late recurrences occur many years later, so lifelong follow-up is essential.
pitfalls: Mistaking the mass for a benign inflammatory nasal polyp, delaying diagnosis and biopsy
Interpreting the biopsy as another small round blue cell tumour without a neuroendocrine immunohistochemistry panel
Relying on CT alone and underestimating intracranial or orbital extension that MRI would reveal
Failing to survey for late nodal and distant recurrence during follow-up
Leaving positive skull-base margins after resection
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery

NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines: Head and Neck Cancers
management: Early stage disease confined to the nasal or sinonasal cavity (Kadish A/B) can be managed with surgical resection alone, or radiotherapy alone in select cases.

More advanced disease with skull base or intracranial extension (Kadish C) is generally treated with surgical resection aiming for negative skull base margins, most often endoscopic endonasal or open craniofacial resection, followed by postoperative radiotherapy.

Disease with cranial nerve involvement, invasion near the optic chiasm, or cavernous or sphenoid sinus invasion is generally managed with definitive radiotherapy or chemoradiation rather than surgery, and should be planned by a multidisciplinary team.
Elective neck irradiation is recommended even in clinically node negative patients given the meaningful risk of occult cervical nodal spread, and is definitely indicated for nodal disease (Kadish D).

Endoscopic endonasal approaches have largely replaced open craniofacial or bifrontal craniotomy approaches in many cases, with comparable disease control and better functional outcomes, though open resection is still needed for some extensive or recurrent disease.
Skull base reconstruction (for example with a pericranial, nasoseptal, or free flap) is planned as part of the same surgical procedure.
For unresectable disease or patients unfit for surgery, definitive radiotherapy or chemoradiation is used, with conformal planning to limit injury to the cornea and optic pathways.

Systemic chemotherapy for metastatic or advanced sinonasal disease is extrapolated from the broader sinonasal and neuroendocrine tumour literature rather than ENB specific evidence, and typically involves a platinum agent, sometimes combined with a taxane or other agent, used as induction therapy or concurrently with radiotherapy.

No specific systemic regimen is validated for ENB itself, so systemic therapy selection should be individualised by a multidisciplinary head and neck oncology team rather than treated as a fixed protocol.

Recurrent disease after surgery alone is generally managed with chemoradiation or craniofacial resection plus postoperative radiotherapy, while radiotherapy failures may be salvaged with maxillectomy or craniofacial resection where feasible.
Surveillance should be prolonged beyond the typical two to three years used for other head and neck cancers, given the tendency for late local recurrence and delayed cervical nodal metastasis.
Follow-up includes nasal endoscopy and imaging of both the primary site and the neck, with a low threshold to re-image for new cranial nerve symptoms, headache, proptosis, or a neck mass.
Any suspected or confirmed case should be referred promptly to a tertiary head and neck oncology centre with dedicated skull base surgery, neurosurgery, and radiation oncology expertise.

Multidisciplinary discussion is warranted before finalising a treatment plan whenever there is cranial nerve involvement, invasion near the optic chiasm or cavernous or sphenoid sinus, vision threatening orbital disease, or nodal or distant disease.
